site.title: Scaling AI Systems
site.tagline: What breaks between the pilot and the ten-thousandth user.
site.audience: Engineering leaders past MVP, hitting scale problems
site.description: Case studies and cost anatomies for teams that cleared the proof-of-concept stage and are now finding out what only shows up at real scale.

articles.title: When Code Replaces Departments
articles.hook: Scaling AI isn't a model problem; it's a boundary problem. When an agent's output volume rivals a department, the wall between platform engineering and business operations collapses.

articles.title: Who Owns the Agent?
articles.hook: Scaling AI is not a compute problem; it is an orchestration boundary problem.

articles.title: Who Signed Off?
articles.hook: The audit gap isn't a compliance problem — it's an architecture problem. You cannot retroactively inspect what you didn't instrument at the point of decision.

articles.title: The Ownership Void
articles.hook: Org design for AI systems fails when treated as a tooling problem rather than an authority boundary problem.

articles.title: Leverage Lost
articles.hook: AI vendor lock-in isn't a contract trap; it's an architectural one. Your prompts are fused to a single latent space.

articles.title: The Sandbox Lie
articles.hook: Pilot reliability is a structural illusion. The failures that destroy AI systems at scale do not exist in a sandbox—they require the permission scope and volume of production to physically manifest.

articles.title: Own the Front Door
articles.hook: Centralizing AI ownership creates a bottleneck, not a center of excellence — the iteration loop needs to live where domain context lives.

articles.title: The Hostage Architecture
articles.hook: Vendor lock-in in AI extends far beyond data-egress fees; it functions as a subsidized unit-economics trap and a cognitive-calcification crisis.

articles.title: Cheap Tokens, Massive Bills
articles.hook: Dropping unit token prices do not reduce your cloud bill; they lower the barrier for product teams to introduce context payloads and autonomous multi-turn loops that multiply token volume exponentially.

articles.title: The Three-Team Trap
articles.hook: The platform-team inflection arrives when duplicated AI infrastructure across teams costs more than a platform team — and that crossover happens at three teams, not ten.

articles.title: The Audit Bill Nobody Budgeted
articles.hook: AI compliance at scale is an infrastructure cost that compounds with time and volume — and by the time it surfaces in legal's budget, retrofitting costs 10x what building it in would have.

articles.title: Five Teams, Zero Owners
articles.hook: Your org chart assumes one owner per system. Agents have five.

articles.title: The Eval Mirage
articles.hook: Eval coverage isn't a test-suite problem; it's a sampling problem. A 2,000-case suite has an 18% chance of even containing a 1-in-10,000 failure — while production serves that failure 100 times a day.

articles.title: Who Gets Paged for Wrong?
articles.hook: Quality incidents aren't a monitoring problem; they're an ownership problem. Your AI system has an on-call rotation for being down and nobody on call for being wrong — so wrong runs for weeks.

articles.title: The Cache Hit Bill
articles.hook: Your inference bill isn't set by the model's price; it's set by your cache hit rate — and that rate is set by how many teams can edit the prompt prefix. Below about 22%, caching costs more than it saves.

articles.title: The Residency Tax
articles.hook: Data residency isn't a legal checkbox; it's a capacity-partitioning decision. Every region you promise splits your quota, your cache and your failover — and four regions can cost about a quarter more capacity than one pool.

articles.title: Quota Is an Org Chart
articles.hook: Rate limits aren't a vendor constraint; they're an internal allocation problem. Providers meter the organisation, not the team — so one unscheduled batch job can throttle more than a quarter of your customer-facing traffic.

articles.title: Rent, Reserve, or Call
articles.hook: Self-hosting isn't a cost decision; it's a utilization bet. At on-demand H100 prices, a 70B model at 1,500 tokens/s never beats a $1-per-million API — with a 3-year commitment, it needs 70% sustained utilization.
